::: {.fi-standfirst}
**FRESH** starts where most health tools stop: what to do when credible sources
disagree. It re-checks what published studies actually show, reconciles expert
rating systems that contradict each other, and estimates risk for particular people
and places instead of a national average. The statistics are the spine of it. A
number without its uncertainty is not an answer, so the doubt stays on the face of
every result, and nothing counts as settled here until it reproduces a published
benchmark, standard error included.

What people believe is data too. Beliefs steer which questions get funded and who
ends up better off for the science, so we measure them against the expert record.
The gaps come back specific: foods the public judges harshly that the evidence
treats kindly, foods it lets off easy, and the ones the experts cannot agree on
either. That is an education agenda, food by food, rather than a scolding.

Food comes first because that is where expert systems clash most openly and public
belief has drifted furthest. The same methods reach the rest of a life: sleep,
movement, mind and mood, social connection and loneliness, self-care, substance
use, biological age, health literacy, and the place you live, read from what you
report, what you wear, and what your blood says.

Health effort goes to widening access, to definition fights that burn political
capital over what counts as ultraprocessed, to narrow policies that work as
bandages, to pointing at personal behavior, while the information itself gets
treated as solved. It is not. Better
information cures nothing on its own, but it is the cheapest lever almost nobody is
pulling. The tools and essays here are open to anyone who wants to see the evidence
for themselves.
:::
